segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they could go and anoint him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were saying to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who will roll the stone away from the entrance of the tomb for us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away—for it was very large.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look—the place where they laid him.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them. And they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. ⟦But they reported briefly to those around Peter everything they had been commanded. And after this, Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.⟧

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: ⟦Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went and reported it to those who had been with him, as they were mourning and weeping.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he appeared in a different form to two of them as they were walking, on their way into the country.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They too went back and reported it to the rest, but they did not believe them either.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Later he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had been raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new languages;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: they will pick up snakes, and if they drink anything deadly it will certainly not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will get well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then the Lord Jesus, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went out and proclaimed everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.⟧

notes.note: The Sabbath ended at sunset on Saturday, so the women could buy spices that evening and set out at first light on Sunday. Anointing a body with aromatic oils was a last act of honor to the dead, not embalming.

Mark calls the figure simply a young man. Jewish writings of the period often describe angels as young men in bright or white clothing, and Matthew's parallel account calls the figure an angel. Most interpreters therefore take Mark to mean a heavenly messenger, and his words are marked as an angel's here.

notes.traditional: He is risen / He has risen
notes.note: The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive, “he has been raised” (that is, by God), or as an intransitive, “he has risen.” Both are grammatically sound and translations divide; the passive is chosen here because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus.
This refers back to Jesus' words on the way to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:28): “After I am raised, I will go ahead of you to Galilee.”

The double brackets mark text that is almost certainly not part of Mark's original Gospel. The two oldest complete manuscripts end at “for they were afraid.” The bracketed sentences here, known as the Shorter Ending, appear in only a handful of manuscripts, usually followed by verses 9–20, and their vocabulary is unlike Mark's. Scholars debate whether Mark meant to end at verse 8 or whether an original ending was lost.

notes.phrase: Now when he had risen early
notes.note: Verses 9–20, the Longer Ending, are double-bracketed because the two oldest complete manuscripts lack them, and some early Christian writers reported that many Greek copies known to them did too. The passage is found in the great majority of later manuscripts and was known by the late second century. Its style differs from the rest of Mark, and it seems to summarize appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. Most scholars consider it an early addition rather than Mark's own work.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

The traditional rendering is “new tongues.” The Greek word means the tongue as an organ and, by extension, a language; “tongues” in this sense is now archaic in English outside church usage. “Languages” gives what a first-century reader would have heard, though the nature of the speech meant is debated. Some manuscripts lack the word “new.”

candidates.reason: “Tongues” versus “languages” for inspired speech recurs in Acts and 1 Corinthians and should not vary from book to book.
The passive forms used of Jesus' resurrection can be “was raised” or “rose,” and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
Translators alternate between “preach” and “proclaim,” and the cognate noun κήρυγμα (here “proclamation”) should match.
The verb covers rescue, healing and final salvation, so a policy is needed on when to use “save,” “heal” or “rescue.”
Dining posture is rendered variously as “recline,” “sit at table” or “eat,” and the choice should be consistent across the Gospels.
